cards.back: Personal obligation: 'to have to do something.' The subject of *tener* is the person who is obligated.
cards.grammarNote: tener que + infinitive = a specific person must do something. Example: *Jeffrey tiene que arreglar el bug* = Jeffrey has to fix the bug.

cards.back: Impersonal obligation: 'one must / it is necessary to.' No specific subject — applies to anyone.
cards.grammarNote: *Hay* is the impersonal form of *haber*; it does not change for person or number. *Hay que hacer el deploy* = Someone / we / one must do the deploy.

cards.front: Conjugate 'tener que' for all persons (present tense)
cards.back:
yo → tengo que
tú → tienes que
él/ella → tiene que
nosotros → tenemos que
vosotros → tenéis que
ellos/ellas → tienen que
cards.grammarNote: *Tener* is irregular in first person (yo tengo) and stem-changes e→ie in all other present forms except nosotros/vosotros.

cards.front: I have to fix the bug before the standup.
cards.back: Tengo que arreglar el bug antes del standup.
cards.grammarNote: *Tengo que* = I have to; first-person singular obligation. *Antes del* = before the (contraction of *antes de + el*).

cards.front: You have to review the pull request.
cards.back: Tienes que revisar el pull request.
cards.grammarNote: *Tienes que* = you have to (informal tú). Used when speaking directly to a teammate.

cards.front: Jeffrey has to deploy the code today.
cards.back: Jeffrey tiene que desplegar el código hoy.
cards.grammarNote: *Tiene que* = he/she has to; third person singular. *Desplegar* = to deploy (stem-changing e→ie verb).

cards.front: We have to launch the app this Friday.
cards.back: Tenemos que lanzar la aplicación este viernes.
cards.grammarNote: *Tenemos que* = we have to; first person plural. *Este viernes* = this Friday (with demonstrative *este*).

cards.front: They have to finish the feature by tomorrow.
cards.back: Tienen que terminar la función para mañana.
cards.grammarNote: *Tienen que* = they have to; third person plural. *Para mañana* = by/for tomorrow — *para* indicates a deadline.

cards.front: Someone has to do the deploy. (impersonal)
cards.grammarNote: *Hay que* does not change — always third person singular impersonal. Compare: *Tenemos que hacer el deploy* (we have to) vs. *Hay que hacer el deploy* (it must be done).

cards.front: The code must be reviewed before deploying. (impersonal)
cards.back: Hay que revisar el código antes de desplegar.
cards.grammarNote: *Antes de + infinitive* = 'before doing something.' *Hay que* sets an impersonal rule that applies to the team.

cards.front: The server needs to be configured. (impersonal)
cards.grammarNote: Use *hay que* when the speaker doesn't specify who is responsible, or when issuing a general instruction to the team.

cards.front: Jeffrey does not have to go into the office.
cards.back: Jeffrey no tiene que ir a la oficina.
cards.grammarNote: *No tiene que* = 'does not have to' (no obligation). Do not confuse with *no debe* (must not / should not).

cards.front: Jeffrey had to fix a critical bug yesterday.
cards.back: Jeffrey tuvo que arreglar un error crítico ayer.
cards.grammarNote: *Tuvo que* = preterite of *tener que*: 'had to.' *Tener* is highly irregular in the preterite: tuve, tuviste, tuvo, tuvimos, tuvieron.

cards.front: What is the difference? 'Hay que estudiar' vs. 'Tengo que estudiar'
cards.back:
'Hay que estudiar' = One must study / Studying is necessary. (impersonal)
'Tengo que estudiar' = I have to study. (personal obligation)
cards.grammarNote: *Hay que* is impersonal and does not target a specific person. *Tener que* always has a personal subject — it changes with each person.

cards.front: In a standup: 'We need to fix the bug before the client sees it.' (impersonal style)
cards.back: Hay que arreglar el bug antes de que el cliente lo vea.
cards.grammarNote: *Antes de que* + subjunctive: 'before the client sees it' — *vea* is subjunctive of *ver*. *Hay que* sets the team-level obligation.
